prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, which brought optical frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B010 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part. After the first round I looked for what could move me, and the exchange mostly sharpened the case. The core experimental facts are not disputed by anyone. Magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be interrogated while light shift, Doppler and recoil shifts are controlled, and the resulting clocks reach about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, with independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL agreeing across laboratories. That is the test I apply to any experimental claim, and it is met. The capability is already producing physics, namely relativistic redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and spin-exchange and many-body effects in the clock ensemble, so this is not only a better number. On attribution I would now word the citation around the lattice scheme and the 1e-18 regime, which is where Katori (concept and first demonstrations) and Ye (accuracy, stability, many-body regime) are decisive and distinct, and which keeps the text accurate about Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups, who are not named.
statement.case_against: The reservations raised in round 1, which I share, are not answered by repetition. The strongest is distinctness. The comb (2005) and ion control (2012) are enabling tools for optical clocks and the lattice clock is the next step in that lineage, so a critic can say we would be rewarding a refinement. My answer is that those prizes honoured the ruler and the single-ion system, while the lattice scheme is a different physical route that changes what is measurable, but I accept this is a judgement and not a fact. Second, this is a measurement capability and not a surprise in nature, and I must not let my own preference for instruments decide that question for the committee. Third, credit outside the two names is real, and the SI second is not yet redefined, so part of the impact is prospective. I do not think the redefinition should be part of the case.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a discovery made in nature, and in his uncertainties asks whether a precision-measurement achievement should be preferred when attribution is cleaner, and elsewhere what the clock has revealed that earlier clocks could not.
responses.response: I take the discovery-in-nature argument seriously, and the 2013 diffuse flux is a secure detection. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: I cannot see which three of a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND forerunners, are decisive for the 2013 observation, and most of the flux is still unattributed. On your question about the clock, the concrete answer is that 1e-18 clocks resolve gravitational time dilation over a millimetre, set tight limits on drifting constants and expose collective spin-exchange effects in a lattice, none of which earlier clocks could reach. So it has already revealed physics, even if it is not a new particle or source. I would not move without the expert reports saying who was decisive for IceCube.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from twisted bilayer graphene to B010, but asks whether the 1e-18 claims for strontium lattice clocks are independent of blackbody-shift and lattice-light-shift systematics, and worries he is joining a consensus.
responses.response: The blackbody shift was the dominant limitation until it was attacked directly, by controlling and measuring the radiation environment of the atoms (cryogenic and in situ characterisation at JILA and in other strontium clocks) and by calculating the dynamic polarisability. The agreement between clocks with different geometries and different treatments of the blackbody and lattice light shift is the real check, because a common-mode error would not cancel in the comparison. The remaining question is higher-order light shifts, which are bounded by varying the lattice depth. I think your move is on scientific grounds and not just consensus. On B051 I agree that a materials discovery is a legitimate alternative, but the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and Fatemi make the attribution much harder than for the clock.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B047 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for a complete theory-to-experiment chain, and concedes that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan sit outside his allocation and that the 2016 prize overlaps.
responses.response: I respect the clean mechanism, and the independent transport and ARPES confirmations are the kind of reproducibility I trust. My problem remains the third name. Dropping Hasan removes the 3D line, and dropping Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang removes the people who told Molenkamp which quantum well to grow, so any three-person prize would be contested for years. A prize with two names and no serious priority dispute is easier to defend, and I think it is also the more honest option. I would ask you what citation wording would stop B047 being read as only an addition to the 2016 prize.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B010 but admits that a clock is a measurement capability and not a surprise about nature, and asks that the atomic-structure theory behind the systematics and the pending SI redefinition be kept separate from the core case.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The atomic-structure calculations of magic wavelengths and blackbody and higher-order shifts are part of why the 1e-18 uncertainty budget can be trusted, so the citation should speak of the invention and the regime and not of the redefinition of the second. I would also state openly in the committee text that this is a measurement-physics prize, so that nobody can claim we hid it. I do not think that lowers its standing: the physics content is the new regime of controlled many-body systems read out with extreme precision.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, prefers B010 after leaving IceCube as an alternative, and asks whether the committee has room for a lattice-clock prize next to 2005 and 2012 and whether the redefinition of the second should weigh on timing.
responses.response: Your question on the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the right one, and I would answer it with the citation: naming the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime makes the object of the prize different from the comb and the single ion. On timing, I do not think we should wait for the redefinition. The science does not depend on it, and a committee that delays for an administrative decision of the CIPM is making a different kind of judgement. My own earlier remark on this was too close to treating the redefinition as evidence of impact, and I withdraw that emphasis.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations and Ye for the accuracy and many-body regime, and how they weigh Takamoto, Lemonde and the Kimble-era discussion.
Whether a majority regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, even with the citation worded around the lattice scheme.
Whether a measurement-capability prize should take precedence over a discovery in nature, which is a committee judgement I cannot settle by experimental evidence alone.

For my alternatives, whether circuit QED (B041) is too close to the 2025 prize and whether the five-name Hubbard-simulation credit (B019) can be restricted to three without excluding Zoller and Cirac.
statement.conflict_note: No decisive conflict. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, the JILA environment of Jun Ye, but I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye and no current tie to either. My WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers, which bears on my alternative B041 and not on my preferred B010. I see no reason for my recusal on B010, and I would be willing to discount my view if the committee judged the JILA connection relevant.
